emergency-fund.question: What is an emergency fund mainly for?
emergency-fund.explanation: It's cash set aside for surprises — a job loss, a medical bill, a car repair — kept easy to access rather than invested for growth.

apy.question: What does APY (Annual Percentage Yield) tell you?

options.b: The real yearly return including compounding

apy.explanation: APY factors in compounding, so it reflects what you actually earn over a year — a more honest number than a flat interest rate.

needs-vs-wants.question: Which of these is usually a "need" rather than a "want"?
needs-vs-wants.explanation: Needs keep you housed, fed, and functioning. Wants improve life but aren't essential — the distinction is the backbone of most budgets.

50-30-20.question: In the 50/30/20 budgeting rule, what does the 20% go toward?
50-30-20.explanation: The split is roughly 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings/debt — a simple starting framework, not a strict rule.

compound-interest.question: Why does starting to save early matter so much?

options.a: Compound interest earns returns on your past returns too
options.b: Banks pay more to new savers
options.c: Prices only go up early in the year

compound-interest.explanation: Each period, interest is earned on your original amount AND everything it already earned — the growth accelerates the longer it runs.

budgeting-basics.question: What is the main point of tracking every expense?

options.b: To see where money actually goes

budgeting-basics.explanation: Most people underestimate small recurring spending until they track it — the goal is visibility, not judgment.

credit-score.question: Which habit most consistently helps a credit score?
credit-score.explanation: Payment history is typically the single biggest factor — consistent on-time payments matter more than any single trick.

diversification.question: What problem does diversification mainly solve?

options.b: Reducing the impact of any one investment doing badly

diversification.explanation: Spreading money across different assets means one bad performer doesn't sink the whole picture. It manages risk, not returns.

inflation.question: What does inflation do to cash sitting idle?
inflation.explanation: If prices rise faster than your cash earns interest, the same pile of money buys a little less each year.

debt-snowball.question: In the "debt snowball" method, which debt do you pay off first?
debt-snowball.explanation: Snowball targets the smallest balance first for quick wins and momentum — a different debt method (avalanche) targets highest interest instead.

opportunity-cost.question: What does "opportunity cost" mean when spending money?

options.a: The tax you pay on a purchase
options.b: What you give up by not using that money elsewhere
options.c: A store’s markup on an item

opportunity-cost.explanation: Every dollar spent one way is a dollar that can’t go toward something else — the real cost includes what you didn’t get to do instead.

net-worth.question: How is net worth calculated?

options.b: What you own minus what you owe

net-worth.explanation: Net worth is a snapshot: everything you own (assets) minus everything you owe (debts). Income is a flow; net worth is a total.

automatic-savings.question: Why do automatic transfers to savings tend to work well?

options.a: They remove the need to decide every time
options.b: They earn a legally guaranteed higher rate
options.c: They are required by most banks

automatic-savings.explanation: Automating "pays yourself first" before you can spend it — it turns saving into a default instead of a decision you have to keep making.

high-yield-savings.question: What mainly distinguishes a high-yield savings account from a regular one?

options.a: It has no withdrawal limits at all
options.b: It pays a meaningfully higher interest rate
options.c: It doubles as a checking account

high-yield-savings.explanation: The core difference is the interest rate — often several times a standard savings account — usually offered by online-first banks.

index-funds.question: What does an index fund do?

options.b: Tracks a broad market index as a whole

index-funds.explanation: Rather than betting on individual companies, an index fund holds a broad slice of the market, spreading risk across many holdings at once.
